name: Eszopiclone
lead: Eszopiclone, sold as Lunesta and as generics, is a prescription nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic of the cyclopyrrolone class. It is the active (S)-enantiomer of zopiclone and is used for insomnia in adults.[1]

The FDA approved it in December 2004. It is a Schedule IV controlled substance in the US, and the FDA added a boxed warning in 2019 about serious injuries from complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking.[1]
Eszopiclone has no approved appearance use and no published studies of appearance outcomes. It is mentioned here as part of the sleep-medicine landscape that some people connect with recovery.

paras: Eszopiclone is indicated for the treatment of insomnia in adults.[1][2] The American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline for chronic insomnia assessed individual drugs including eszopiclone.[3]

Its hypnotic effect is believed to arise from interaction with GABA-A receptor complexes near or coupled to benzodiazepine binding sites, enhancing inhibitory neurotransmission; the precise mechanism is described as unknown.[1][2] It is rapidly absorbed and has a half-life of about six hours.[1]

Labelled risks include CNS depression with next-day impairment, complex sleep behaviors (sleep-driving, sleepwalking), abnormal thinking or hallucinations, and worsening depression or suicidal ideation.[1][2] The FDA lowered the recommended starting dose in 2013 and added a boxed warning in 2019.[1] As a Schedule IV drug it carries risks of abuse, dependence and withdrawal.[1]

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study tested nightly eszopiclone for six months in adults with chronic insomnia.[4] Other studies examined co-administration with fluoxetine in insomnia with major depression, and effects on respiratory arousal threshold in obstructive sleep apnoea.[5][6] A registered trial compared eszopiclone with zopiclone.[10]

A network meta-analysis in The Lancet compared pharmacological treatments for acute and long-term insomnia.[7] A matched cohort study associated hypnotic use with higher mortality, and reviews discuss safety in older adults; observational findings cannot establish cause.[8][9] No studies of appearance outcomes were found.

timeline.event: FDA adds a boxed warning for complex sleep behaviors.[1]

card.summary: A prescription Z-drug sleeping pill (Lunesta); sleep research only, nothing on appearance.
card.note: Boxed FDA warning for complex sleep behaviors; Schedule IV.

quick.overview:
Eszopiclone (Lunesta) is a prescription Z-drug for insomnia, the active half of zopiclone.

It has not been studied for appearance; the only link is the general role of sleep in recovery.
quick.mechanism: It enhances GABA-A receptor signalling near the benzodiazepine site, producing sedation.
quick.risks: The FDA boxed warning covers complex sleep behaviors such as sleepwalking and sleep-driving; other reported effects include next-day impairment, dependence and mood changes. It is Schedule IV.
